utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber has not heard of any preliminaries to be raised. Therefore, could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Keserovic. I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth and the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Mr. Lukic will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Lukic. If you're ready, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you told us something about Major Malinic telling you at the Nova Kasaba stadium or football pitch, that there were some 2 and a half thousand prisoners. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your testimony of the 12th of June 2013, Major Malinic said the following. I'll read it out. It is the transcript in this case, Wednesday, the 12th of June. I have a four-digit number for the page. Well, I'll provide an exact reference because I seem to be missing a digit. In any case, it is lines 17 through 20. My learned friend, Mr. Vanderpuye asked the following: "Q. Did you have at Nova Kasaba between 1500 and 2.000 prisoners to your recollection at around 5.30 in the afternoon of 13 July 1995? "A. Between 1.000 and 1200 members of the 28th Division were taken prisoner at Kasaba."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting and I think it's just a translation issue because we are getting "that in your testimony," and I'm thinking it's -- it must have been the testimony of Malinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's Major Malinic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I don't know what the witness is getting but we all got that you're referring to his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Witness what was just read to you was the testimony of Mr. Malinic, not your testimony. If there is any misunderstanding, then we stand hereby corrected. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And perhaps you start again with the question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you understand I was reading from Major Malinic's testimony? Is it clear that I was reading from Major Malinic's testimony?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you at the football pitch in Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not at the football pitch in Nova Kasaba. I met with Malinic along the road at the fork towards the school where the MP Battalion was, not at the football pitch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, Madam Registrar informed me that you were reading from transcript page 12611, lines 17 to 20. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you allow for the possibility that you either misheard what Major Malinic told you or that you remembered it incorrectly, since that information seems to have come from him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Anything is possible. That is an improperly phrased question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I could answer that question. You could never exclude for the possibility that. This is common knowledge, I would say. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you allow for the possibility that Major Malinic was in a better position to describe the number of people who were held at the football pitch in Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the same. I can answer that question. But everyone could allow for that possibility. Of course, there is a strong suggestion that therefore it's better. The Chamber of course will have to consider that. But to ask this witness whether you could exclude the possibility that someone knew better, of course you can't. It's a useless question. Please proceed. It's argumentative to some extent because what you would say, and that's perhaps a very valid argument, if he was closer, if he was there, would he be in a better position. Don't ask this witness. Make it a valid argument perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But we heard this question like this pretty often in this trial, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And usually there was not made many objections to it. Now, objections are made to it and I think that's the right time to tell everyone who wants to put a similar question that it's a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if I can add to that, don't hesitate to make objections to some of the questions by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another thing you testified to as Major Malinic having told you is a situation where, in your words, Major Malinic told you that General Mladic came along and told him to stop making lists of those captured at Nova Kasaba. You do recall having testified to that effect on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When the commander of the Main Staff came along, General Mladic, that is, the making of lists or the process of registration was halted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We know you were not present when it happened since at the time you were not in the area of Srebrenica. I wanted to read out to you what Major Malinic said the other day on the 12th of June this year. When asked to describe it by my learned friend, Mr. Vanderpuye, he indeed provided an answer on page 12607. I was working on it last night, so there seems to be some confusion with the numbers. Perhaps 13607. In any case, I will provide the exact reference later on as well. Starting with line 2. "Q. And when General Mladic arrived at Nova Kasaba and addressed the prisoners, was the process of making a list of prisoners ongoing?" Major Malinic answered: "A. The process of making a list lasted from the moment of capture until the soldiers of the 28th Division went off in buses and trucks. When General Mladic happened to be at the stadium, he addressed the prisoners and at that point in time, the taking down of the names of the prisoners had to be interrupted because he was addressing all members of the 28th Division at the stadium or at the pitch."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, this is on page 12607.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that moment, Major Malinic abandons the topic, but on the next page, 12608, Judge Orie asked, taking him back to the topic, in line 10. So Judge Orie's question: "After Mr. Mladic had addressed the persons on this football pitch, was then the listing of names continued? "A. I think that it did. There was no reason why the process of listing prisoners should not continue." [Interpretation] I wanted to ask you this: Did you ask for an additional explanation as to whether the making of lists continued after General Mladic's departure?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall whether I sought additional information as to whether it was continued. What I learned was that lists were being made until General Mladic arrived and that it was interrupted at that point. I have no recollection of anything pertaining to the continuation of that process.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry but my question was whether you asked him if they continued, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, that question was answered. It started with, "I do not recall that I sought additional information." That is asking for more information. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you familiar with or did you learn at a later stage that Major Malinic did not have sufficient means to provide security for the prisoners so that they could stay in the same location during the night? He did not have a fence, he did not have enough men to guard the perimeter, he did not have lights: Did you learn anything to that effect?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of numbers and amount of resources, that's really something I can't testify to at this point. But based on the documents about the situation in the military police units, one could see that among other units, the MP Battalion of the Main Staff did not have sufficient resources. In terms of shortage of soldiers, I was aware of it because the company undergoing training was also used to be assigned to the blockade of a part of the road between Nova Kasaba and Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said that Major Malinic told you that he was told by General Mladic that the people from the football pitch would be transferred to Bratunac. Perhaps briefly we can look at P1574 in e-court. It is the interview of Major Malinic. We are only interested in two lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 26, lines 8 and 9 in both versions. It is the good page in English but I don't see it in the B/C/S version. This is not the right page. Yet, this morning when I counted the pages, both versions had it on page 26 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll read out from the English so that you receive interpretation. [In English] "And did you know where these prisoners were being taken to?" Answer: "No." [Interpretation] According to the interview provided by Major Malinic, he himself did not know. He had no information where the prisoners were to be transferred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it's not the same. Of course, I've not the whole of the statement on my mind at this moment, but what someone tells you that will happen and what then happens are two different things. Please keep that in mind. Therefore, you're not reflecting the evidence accurately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And we have the relevant page now on the screen and in B/C/S -- in B/C/S too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we do have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: These are lines 12 and 13 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I have to read the context to know exactly, but if you single out two lines, where someone is taken or where someone says people are to be taken is not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since the question seems to follow the line -- the previous line of questioning, in terms of some issues that we were instructed not to ask about, I'll change topics. I wanted to ask you something about the MUP units that were present in the area at the time. Although I am aware of the fact that you weren't there and I don't know how privy you were to the operation that was carried out. However, I have a few general questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That misstates the evidence. He was there, if you're talking about the Bratunac area, so I -- I don't know what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, I was thinking about the dates. Since I'm going to ask about the 11th of July, that he was not in that area at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I agree with that. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I wasn't precise enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've accepted the apologies, I take it. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So between the 6th and 11 July, you were not in Srebrenica or in the area of Srebrenica and I am aware of it, but did you know that the MUP units which arrived in the area were not placed within the communications system used by the Drina Corps in that operation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that according to the law on home affairs, the MUP units do retain the autonomy of command in combat activities as well? Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with the ways and means through which the MUP units may be placed under the command of the commander of a given operation, and this is solely pursuant to a written decision issued by the Minister of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your work in cooperation with the commission for investigations into Srebrenica, did you ever come across such a document whereby the MUP units were engaged in Krivaja 95 and subordinated to the command of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, were there problems encountered in the use of police units in the course of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were. And quite frequently. Precisely for the fact that there was a need to have them involved in specific operations, and due to the fact that they were even present in the area where they were supposed to be engaged, there were frequent and almost regular occurrences where, before such use, they had to wait for four to five days before such a decision was issued. I, myself, had experience in having to involve these units, but they could not be involved before the minister had produced such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that these units never fit into the military structure properly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to draw a generally acceptable conclusion. What I know from my practical experience is that we were two different systems that were at odds on many issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about the role of the security organs in the work of the military police. Is it correct that some of the duties incumbent upon the security organ may be delegated to the military police and that he may ask them to perform these tasks without asking the commander for the permission to do so?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I spoke about it too. These are specific tasks and duties arising primarily from the purview of the services we referred to, crime prevention services, pre-criminal charges, inquiries and the involvement of military courts, and some other affairs from the purview of these services. The chief of the security organ could assign such tasks to a unit of the military police that fell within his command or his HQ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The other aspect of the role of the security organs in the military police is that of a deputy commander for -- assistant commander for security, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what is his specific role in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His role is multi-fold. He will issue proposals for the decision of the commander and will propose various ways and means of using the military police that the commander will then decide upon. He's also to monitor the ways in which the military police unit is performing the task that it was given by the commander. As assistant commander, he's also responsible for combat readiness. That's to say the combat readiness of that unit, its level of training, that it -- making sure that it is properly equipped. And all these tasks are ones that the security organ will have in respect of a military police unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The third role of a security organ in my understanding is -- is drafting orders, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as an organ down the professional line, the security organ will draft that part of the order that will relate to the use of the military police unit. It is up to the commander to then subsequently accept it or modify it, and then issue an order that he sees fit. At any rate, these professional organs, specialist organs, are there to draft all the documents that a commander is entitled to issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is the relationship between the security organ at the brigade level and the security organ in the Main Staff? Is that relationship a direct one or must it actually necessarily go through the security organ at corps level?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where the brigade is part of a corps, there will certainly not be a direct relationship between the security organ at brigade level and that of the Main Staff. Rather, it will go through the security organ at corps level.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Specifically speaking, Colonel Beara of the Main Staff, could he directly contact Momir Nikolic of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the rules that were in force, he was not able to and he was not supposed to. It may have so happened in practice that a certain level would be side-stepped but that was not proper. It was not to be done that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Under the rules in force, is it also the case that this could not work the other way around either? That's to say, Momir Nikolic could not have contacted directly Colonel Beara, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a question in that respect to the witness? The question about making contact up the line or down the line is not very specific. Could you explain what is your understanding of having contact or making contact in comparison to issuing orders and reporting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood Mr. Lukic's question to mean that contact meant issuing orders and reporting. That's how I understood the term "contact" in the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yesterday, you testified about the professional duties of the security organs of different levels in the VRS. In professional terms, in comparison to command responsibility, was it possible to have direct contact between the different levels, the security organs in different levels of the units? I'm not talking about orders now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Professional duties would also be dealt with at appropriate levels. Security administration, then the corps security organ, and then down the chain to the brigades; and the other way around, reporting from the brigade up to the corps and from the corps to the staff. So that would apply to professional duties too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you saying that there was no contact between the security organs of different levels, brigade, corps, and Main Staff? That means without going through the commanders of the different levels.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They did have contact, but official contacts and professional duties were dealt with always by the superior security organ contacting the one immediately the level down, and, of course, going up the chain, it would be the security organ at a certain level contacted -- contacting the immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is the immediate superior in that respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we are talking about the security issues related to the staff, the chief of security of a -- of the command which is immediately superior would be the immediate superior. If we have the chief of security of a brigade reporting, he will be reporting to the chief of security of the corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd like us to briefly discuss command over the military police. Who is in command of the military police, say in the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The company commander or the MP company commander or the MP platoon commander will be the immediate commander, and he will receive his orders from the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Under the rules, was it possible for Vujadin Popovic to come from the Drina Corps and have under his command the military police of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that Colonel Beara of the Main Staff was not able to have command over the military police of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who proposes to the commander of the Bratunac Brigade the ways in which the military police would be used?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of security of the brigade; in the instant case, Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to the rules, was it possible for Momir Nikolic to communicate independently and have direct dealings with Popovic and Beara without consulting and receiving permission from the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not quite clear about the tasks that you are referring to. They could resolve issues from the sole jurisdiction of security organs, that is to say certain counterintelligence issues together. In that situation, they would be able to meet all three of them. However, when it comes to the command of a military police unit, they could not do so under no circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are nearing the end. Bear with me for a moment to check if I have any questions left for you. Let's briefly look at another document that you've already been shown. It's P1578. While we are waiting for it, it's a document where one page is handwritten. In the English version, we need page 4, paragraph number 3. In the B/C/S version, we need page 2. That's how it was uploaded in e-court. Paragraph 3. What we see here in this passage, which you say was written by General Mladic, is the following: "No one has the right to either stop or delay, let alone file away in archives, any case. No one is or can be so wealthy so as to be above the law. Anyone who breaks the law and commits a punishable act must be held responsible. Commanders do not have the right to prevent security organs and members of the military police from doing their duties. On the contrary, they are duty-bound to assist them as much as they can." In the work of security affairs, and even previously, this document is dated -- just a moment. It's dated back to the period immediately preceding the events in Srebrenica. Were you ever in a situation to come across security organs preventing their own subordinates from performing their duties, any such irregularities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this document dates back to March of 1995. As I said yesterday, I participated in its drafting once the situation was assessed. There were cases, and this made the situation more difficult for security organs and military police services in their attempts to resolve cases, especially the perpetration of crimes in the area of responsibility of these units. Very frequently political interests and influences would clash on this score, where political leaders in a certain community would have requests of the army not to investigate certain cases. Now, under the Law on Criminal Procedure, the police was bound to document and investigate and report on anything that came to its notice, everything had -- every such act or crime had to be dealt with through to the end. In our reports, I think we did cite specific examples where units encountered problems in investigating misconduct and crimes, and I believe that item 3, as it is worded, was formulated as a result of all these events, as it was worded by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your line of work, did you gain the impression that General Mladic sought at any point in time privileges for himself or to be placed above the law?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not gain such an impression, but then I wasn't really someone who could grant him any sort of privileges. The only thing that I could do as a commander was to discharge my duties as best as I could, if that could be considered some sort of privilege for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me finish with a rather marginal question. You were asked if Colonel Beara was loyal to General Mladic. You tried to explain this issue but I don't think you finished what you wanted to say, so I'll ask you now: Was it correct that Beara was a superior to General Tolimir in the command of the naval district?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it correct that Beara objected with General Mladic for the fact that Tolimir was now his superior in the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if he said so to General Mladic or not. He didn't do so in my presence. However, I did hear on a couple of occasions Colonel Beara expressing disgruntlement with the fact that the situation was now inverse, and I think that in some of my testimonies, I did mention that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, thank you. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Judge Fluegge has one more questions for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keserovic, I would like to take you back to the issue of the units directly attached to the Main Staff. You testified about that yesterday, especially with respect to the 10th Sabotage Detachment and the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment. Then you were asked by Mr. Lukic, and this can be found on page 12883, in line 15: "Q. In principle, in keeping with the principle of unity of command, would you agree that they were resubordinated to the Drina Corps in that operation?" "That operation" meaning the liberation of Srebrenica. Your answer was, I quote: "All of the units should have and probably were resubordinated to the operations commander; that is to say, the Drina Corps commander. What things were like in the field is something I don't know because I was not a direct participant. In any case, it should have been the way I described." Do you recall your testimony of today -- of yesterday?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do recall it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you please provide me with a reason why that should have been the way that they -- these units had to be subordinated to the Drina Corps commander?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: An operation is a complex combat activity requiring the engagement of several joint tactical --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Joint and tactical units.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true though that operations can be carried out by operational units at the level of corps and up. When it is organised the way Krivaja was, where in addition to the units of the Drina Corps in the operation, there was participation by certain units which did not make part of that unit, then it was obligatory under the principle of unity of command to have all such units resubordinated for the duration of that operation to the operation commander. They were all supposed to have been resubordinated to the Drina Corps commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand, but isn't that also true for units engaged in a certain action and operation, units belonging to the Ministry of Interior, the MUP?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The armed forces in a time of war also encompass MUP units. Those units also should have been resubordinated to the operation commander. I discussed a specific problem in that regard. They would only be resubordinated when ordered in written form by the Minister of the Interior. He was the only person who could order it to them, and then they would be resubordinated to the military commander in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And that would be also in conformity with the principle of unity of command, correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a question related to the last one. You said that it sometimes took days and days before such orders for resubordination were issued. Do you remember how that happened just prior to the Krivaja operation? Was there any specific problem at that point in time, and do you have any recollection on decisions resubordinating the police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, as for any circumstances concerning the assembly of units and resubordination at the time, it is something I don't know about. I have no such information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you do not even know whether the minister of the interior had approved the resubordination?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, not at the time. I don't know what the solution was that was used at the time. I don't know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we are talking about theory, nothing else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I explained how things should have been. Now, what the situation was really like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is what I call theory, how things should be. And how things were, that is facts. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know whether the parties could provide further assistance in relation to the matters I just raised with the witness, not necessarily at this very moment but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart is looking for the document from the minister which has been a long part of the history of this case which should come up, I think, fairly soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Then we'll -- I'm confident that we'll not be left alone with a lack of knowledge. Mr. McCloskey, any questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. But we have, I don't know if you have a subject to deal with in two minutes, that's fine. Otherwise we will take the break first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I know you've seen a lot of documents over the years. Do you recall Mr. Karnavas or anyone showing you a document dated 10 July in the name of Tomo Kovac, the acting minister of interior, which has President Karadzic authorising him to be pulled from the Trnovo battlefield and coming over to the Srebrenica battlefield to report to General Krstic on 11 July?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall having seen that document, but I can't exclude that I have seen it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we try D129.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Might take a moment. We see a 10 July document to the commander of the Special Police Brigade. Is that -- can you remind us what the name of that person was? You've I think mentioned him earlier in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the Special Police Brigade at the time was Goran Saric. The Chief of Staff or his deputy was Colonel Ljubisa Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. It's the deputy that you'd mentioned. Thank you for that correction. And we see here that it says based on the order of the Supreme Commander of the Republika Srpska of the armed forces, and that is who?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the president of the republic, Mr. Karadzic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And he issues this order, and I won't read it all out, but we can see that it's going from one combat operation, it's listing several units, it's appointing Borovcanin the deputy commander of the special brigade, and basically as we see in paragraph 4 he's supposed to go to Bratunac on 11 July. Let's go to the next page. And on arrival at the destination the unit commander shall contact General Krstic. So this is Borovcanin being ordered to report to General Krstic. Now, if, after this, Borovcanin is receiving and following orders from General Mladic, would that be an indication that he was now under the command of the army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By virtue of this order, the commander of MUP forces and the force itself was placed under the command of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. One last question. We see here in one of these paragraphs, if we could go back to the first page, that he is supposed to take some Serbian MUP units from the Trnovo area. Did you ever hear about Borovcanin coming to the Srebrenica area with any Serbian MUP units such as the Kajmen, Plavi, or Skorpioni?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I have no such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, that I think settled that topic for me. I do have several other issues that were brought up that I would like to be able to get into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will do that after the break. Mr. Keserovic, would you please follow the usher? We take a break of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be brought into the courtroom. Mr. McCloskey, could you meanwhile give us an indication of how much time you'd need? I hardly dare to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I was afraid you were going to ask, but I'm -- I have to commit myself. I will, one hour. Hopefully less. But I had -- there was many issues brought up and the resolution of chronology is -- I'm going to make another attempt at, but if I can't do it in an hour, you'll want to throw me out anyway and I'll want to leave. So an hour should do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what they call a win-win situation these days, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Keserovic, you'll now be further re-examined by Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, I want to take another stab at clarifying the chronology and it's -- could we go to your testimony again in Tolimir, at 28995, e-court page 4. This is the part that I had read to you before. I won't read it again. You basically say that after your -- that after your Blagojevic testimony you went back to your notebook, consulted it, and this should be at line 20 in the English -- of course there is only English but -- we see that you consulted your notebook to sort out this dilemma and you went over the notebook again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Chronology of events and the dates that are noted there, although there are dates that were skipped because there were no developments on those days. So based on that, my stay in Bratunac should have been the 17th actually. And then I ask you there, do you still have access to that notebook, and you explain at that point you did not. Well, knowing that were you coming to testify for -- in the trial of General Mladic, did you reassert your efforts to find this notebook that was obviously very important for you in determining this issue?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said already in the Tolimir case that all of the written material and notes of mine were taken away from the office at the moment when I was removed from duty, and it was never returned to me. It includes the small notebook which was taken with the rest of the notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand that. My question was had you made any other efforts, you're a general, a senior officer, to tell anyone that were you coming here to testify and that you needed that notebook?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not do anything in particular in that regard. Seven years is too long a time for me not to have had any access to the armed forces or the Ministry of Defence, and in the meantime there had been a reform and a number of changes. So for the most part, I no longer know any of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, could I ask a question? Has the Prosecution undertaken any effort to get hold of the notebook?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I was asking myself that same question and the answer is no. So the answer would be equally applicable to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, let's go to the day you were in Bratunac to try to -- might help perhaps to sort out some chronology. You had mentioned before that you had stopped by and dealt with some issues relating to wounded, and if we could hopefully save some time by that same 65 ter number, if we could go to, sorry, page 13979 and I don't have the e-court right now, I'm sorry, but let me just ask you -- it should be 33. And you -- this was the question about the wounded, and you may remember Judge Nyambe read back your answer and asked you another question about it. If we look at line -- it should 13979, I'm sorry. 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you again give the number of the 13?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- we have now 13879 and 979 most likely, let me see whether there is -- that's not part of this document because it only has 71 pages, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let me -- sorry, we've had to divide that into another 65 ter and that is 28996. And -- page 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I'll start from page 39 where your answer on a question was: "From the command of the Dutch Battalion --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we wait until we have it on our screens?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are now at 13978. Is that the page? Or did I hear you say 979?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah. Let's start there. That's good. I'll just -- the answer I want is at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where you're asked by me to go back and describe the task of Colonel Jankovic that Tolimir had issued. And then I ask you: "What did you do after that?" And then your answer was: "From the command of the Dutch Battalion, we went again to Bratunac and we stopped by the health centre where the evacuation of prisoners was underway organised by the ICRC. Something was going on there. As we stopped by, somebody, I don't remember who, had separated a group of the wounded. About 20 of them. And these were not evacuated in the organisation of the ICRC. And they eventually stayed there after the column left. And we stayed there and observed until the column of the convoy of the ICRC had left. I remember there was a certain lady, Lucy, organising all this." Is all that -- do you remember all that? Is that all correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do recall that it was so, that the process of evacuating the wounded was underway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where were those wounded from the Bratunac health centre sent to, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where they were taken. There were off-road vehicles there with the sign of the Red Cross. They carried some of them and placed them in the vehicles. Others could walk by themselves. And then they left Bratunac, although I don't know where they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did they go -- did you know whether they went in the direction of Konjevic Polje or the direction of Serbia? If you know.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. If we go down the page a little bit to line 15, we see that you thought that happened in the afternoon around 2.00 or 3.00 p.m. Is that about right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what happened with these -- you say on line 3 -- about 20 of them, of the wounded, were separated and were not sent, where did they go?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ones who stayed behind had not been taken out of the health centre in the first place. So at that point in time, they remained in the health centre in Bratunac. They were not taken in front of the building and left there. They were simply not carried outside at all of the building. They remained inside the health centre, the hospital. But somebody did say that there was a group of around 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And why were they separated?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allegedly, at least from what I could hear from the people there, and from Jankovic, that they were fighters of the 28th Division who had previously committed some crimes, some offences that they should be held liable for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you ever see them shipped out anywhere that day that you were there, these separated men?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 4477.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question. Did you consider them to be prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I considered them to be the wounded. That's what they were referred to, the wounded that were placed in the health centre in Bratunac. I don't know what their status was but they were under the control of the Serb authorities at that time in the health centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were in the territory controlled by Republika Srpska and in the health centre in Bratunac. When the evacuation was taking place, I could see that some were being taken away while others remained, and that there was a circle of people, a group of people, deciding what to do. I didn't get involved in it but from this point I can conclude that there was somebody who made a decision in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That group consisted of what kind of persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Really, some were on stretchers, so there were probably seriously wounded. Others walked by themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said there was a circle of people, a group of people, deciding what to do. My question was, that group of people who decided what to do consisted of what kind of persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I didn't know the people. They were engaged in negotiation with the ICRC representatives who took part in the evacuation. I know that Colonel Jankovic spoke with them as well, but I didn't know the people whatsoever. It was my first time in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Colonel Jankovic was one of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He was present and he was taking part in the conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was he the only military man in that group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say there were no other persons in uniform, be it military or police. But as far as I know, I didn't see any officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How do you know that you didn't see any officers? Where you say, "I can't say there were no other persons in uniform," could that have been officers? Or is it your evidence that foot soldiers were engaged in negotiations with the ICRC? Is that a possibility you want to present to this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were persons in military and police uniforms. I did not observe any visible insignia, be they military or MUP officers. It is also possible that they didn't have the insignia visibly displayed although they held the rank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who told you that they were kept there because they might have committed offences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not sure. I think that I heard this comment from Colonel Jankovic. I believe that he said at some point that there was a request for some of these wounded to be kept behind at the health centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I come back to my previous question. Did you consider them to be prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't hold any specific opinion as to whether they were prisoners of war or possibly the wounded who somehow came to the health centre. How they ended up there, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, apparently most of the wounded were allowed to leave and these were apparently not allowed to leave. Would that make them prisoners of war? Perhaps wounded prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if they had been deprived of their right to be evacuated and taken elsewhere, we may consider them prisoners or soldiers who were stripped of that right. So we may call them prisoners of war and wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Who now took responsibility for those prisoners of war? Who had to take responsibility for those prisoners of war, perhaps should be the first question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were in the hospital for treatment. I don't know if there was any security around the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My first question was who had to take responsibility for those prisoners of war and not to treat them but to be responsible for their fate and for the obligations under the applicable rules?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were already there. Somebody already had some sort of obligation in their respect. It is the commander within whose area of responsibility they are present that is responsible for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who was that in that situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the commander of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So let's look at this ICRC communication to the press, as they call it, basically what we call a press release. It's dated 18 July and it says, ICRC evacuates 88 wounded from Bratunac and Potocari. I'll read it slowly. "Three medical teams of the International Committee of the Red Cross, ICRC, coming from Pale, Bijeljina and Belgrade, evacuated 88 wounded people from Bratunac and Potocari on 17 and 18 July. These casualties, some of them in very serious condition, were taken to Tuzla. Most of them had been previously treated -- most of them had previously been treated at the MSF hospital in Srebrenica. The ICRC conducted this operation with the agreement of General Milan Gvero of the Bosnian Serb Army. When all the wounded had been collected in Bratunac on the first day of the evacuation, 23 of them were refused authorisation to leave. The ICRC considers them to be prisoners of war and noted their identities in order to be able to seek permission to visit them." Is this the situation you just described?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So the ICRC registered these people?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document reads that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you were there. Did you see this bit of registering?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you think it saved their lives?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly, the individuals holding the status of prisoners of war, especially those registered by the ICRC, found salvation in that, regardless of the side they were on, throughout the war in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It goes on to say, in this press release: "The ICRC is also concerned about the fate of thousands of people whose families displaced to Tuzla have lost all track of them. It is requesting the highest Bosnian Serb authorities to give it access to all persons captured during the latest events in Srebrenica." So the ICRC was aware of these missing people. Now they are telling the world about it. Were you aware of it on the 17th of July as well, all the missing men from Srebrenica referred to here?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The day that I was in Bratunac, I didn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 4477 receives number P1580, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would next go to 65 ter 13880.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we are waiting for that, I'll give you a preview. It's from the RS MUP, Ministry of Interior, state security department, from Sarajevo. It is dated 18 July, and it's to the RS deputy minister of interior personally and to the head of the RS MUP Bijeljina, public security department, personally. Now, I don't think I'm going to read the whole thing, but I think if we can take a bit of time to read it, we see that it says on the 17th of July ICRC representatives with the approval of the state and military leadership of Republika Srpska, evacuated 87 wounded and injured Muslim civilians who were accommodated at the UN Dutch Battalion base near Srebrenica and the Bratunac health centre. The Muslims taken charge of were evacuated to Tuzla via Banj Brdo in the Majevica mountains. From among the group of wounded and injured, 23 Muslim men fit for military service were taken out and they will be treated as prisoners of war. Then it talks about filing a criminal report for war crimes and other issues. Then it goes on to describe some of the events. Does this sound like the situation that you experienced, the transport of a number of wounded and the holding back of some 23?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is probably a report about that same activity, the way this is being reported on by the State Security Service of the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've used this word "probably" again. Is there some doubt? It's a pretty specific situation.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I may have used the word "probably" but what we can see from this report is that this is a department of the MUP of Republika Srpska reporting about it, and that it has to do with the situation concerning the evacuation of the wounded from Srebrenica or rather from Bratunac. There is no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So if these two documents are correct, you were present in Bratunac on the 17th of July when these people were evacuated and 23 were separated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to object. This is a misstatement of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I remember well, the ICRC press report says the 17th and the 18th, whereas this report says the 17th. Therefore, there is at least some ambiguity which -- in the way in which you put it to the witness is -- has disappeared. We could have a look. Isn't it true that it says 17th and 18th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then please --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- and there is one more -- one more document that I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you put it to the witness that these two documents, whether he would agree that these two documents clearly point at the 17th. They do not. The second one does, the first one points at the 17th and the 18th. Perhaps a matter to be further explored what happened exactly on the 17th and the 18th, but this is not the way you can put it to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, can you sort it out? Let me see if I can help you and go to one more document. 65 ter -- actually it's P1515, the Judges have seen it before. And this is from the command of the Bratunac Brigade, the intelligence organ, the typewritten name is Momir Nikolic, the handwritten version of it, I'm sure everyone will agree, was in the initials of Radislav Jankovic. And here we see that they are telling the Main Staff intelligence sector in the command of the Drina Corps intelligence department that: "On 18 July at 1515, 22 wounded Muslim prisoners from the 28th Division were evacuated with a police escort provided by the Drina Corps from the health centre in Bratunac. One wounded Muslim remaining out of the 23 remained after the evacuation, which was organised by the ICRC, was handed over to the Zvornik CSB. He's an enemy soldier, Osman Halilovic, concerning whom we had earlier information that he had participated in a massacre of civilians which he himself admitted during the investigation." So earlier you said you didn't know what happened to these 23, now 22. Are these the people from your looking at this document that were separated in your presence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not separated or singled out. I didn't see them. They were put up in the various rooms in the hospital. Mention was made that there were about 20 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you present when they were evacuated?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present when a group was being evacuated, a group of wounded persons, when it was said that a number of them would stay behind in the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And I think we'll recall that you don't know what happened to those that were separated. All right. I think these documents speak for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I can tell you for the record these people were sent to Batkovic and were not -- and did survive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please put your next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've also told us that you met that day in Bratunac with the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, Blagojevic, and he told you something about receiving an order to go to Zepa; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that he was about to go to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you remember what time you -- about what time you saw him at the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime at 11.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. If you give me just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we go to 65 ter 04204. And it should be page 10, but if we could start off with the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a document, sir, that's called the reports of the meeting of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade which the Chamber has seen before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I -- if we go to page -- there we go, thank you for that, so the General can see it. Now if we could go to page 10 in the English, looks like the same in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can see here that on 16 July, the -- under the commander, it says: "Formation of battalion for Zepa by 0700 hours on 17 July 1995." Is that consistent with what you learned from Colonel Blagojevic the next day, on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall him telling me which units or what the strength of the forces leaving the brigade would be. I do know that he told me that he was taking elements of these forces with him and that he was supposed to go to Zepa too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, frankly I'm not sure if this part of the book is in evidence but I'll sort that out for us and let you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we only have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The part you just -- well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I've learned it's only the October reference, you may remember, that's in evidence, and now I would like at least this page in evidence. It's not a huge document, you may want the whole thing, but at least this page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But this comes new. The Defence should have an opportunity to see whether there is any contextualisation needed. Has it been uploaded as a separate page?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not yet. Try to organise that in such a way and meanwhile, Mr. Lukic, if you could think about whether there is any objection, and whether you would need any further pages for contextualisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will have to look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that we'll deal with that after the break then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At least the first page should be included in this collection so we know what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I'll speak to Mr. Lukic. I think it's a small document, I think it's something that is a helpful reference, and we'll decide between ourselves and make you a proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are looking forward to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we go to 65 ter 21063C?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, this will be an intercept that you may remember Mr. Karnavas showing you when you testified as a Defence witness in Blagojevic, and it is from 17 July 1995, and it's a discussion between Badem and Micic. Do you remember what Badem was a code name for?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at this time, no. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think the Defence will probably agree with me on what that code name stands for. It's -- I see Mr. Lukic nodding his head. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then if you tell us what it stands for, then the Chamber also knows what you agree upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is command of Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I agree with Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is hereby on the record. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see that it -- X finally several lines down says: "Go ahead, Badem." And then M says: "Micic, 400 set off." X says: "400?" M says: "Yes, at 1130 hours, the head of the column." "What? "1130 hours." X: "At 1130 hours." M: "The head of the column." X: "How many buses?" M: "Seven buses." X: "How many buses?" "Seven," according to M. X says: "Seven?" M says: "Yes." X says: "Is there anything else?" M says: "(I am leaving) with the last one. "Blagojevic is at the head." X says: "I can't hear you very well." M says: "Blagojevic is at the head. "Hello!" X says: "Yes." M: "Blagojevic, Blagojevic." Then a -- X says: ".... Colonel, Sir." And then M says: "Blagojevic set off at the head." And we can see what the rest of it says. I won't read it all. We see at the end it says: "Hello! Four hundred are on their way." The next page is just a thank you and a bye. Do you remember what you concluded this was about in response to Mr. Karnavas's questions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we concluded at the time that it was a unit of the Bratunac Brigade which set off in the direction of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: With Colonel Blagojevic at its head?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what this participant in the conversation conveyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So would that be consistent with you meeting with Blagojevic at about 11.00 a.m. on the -- and him telling you he was -- received orders to go to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that now brings us back to the old conundrum, who is in command of the -- all the forces with Blagojevic off to Zepa, on the afternoon, early afternoon, of 17 July, who is -- who is in command of those forces?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Zepa is within the area. It is not outside of it. And it's not far. So the time during which Blagojevic was absent was somebody else in command of the forces? I don't know. But one cannot conclude on the basis of this that Blagojevic was not in command of the forces within the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, no one is asking you to draw any conclusions. What you know, you tell us, and when you don't know, tell us as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's see another document, 65 ter 04081. Oh, I'm sorry, I would offer this intercept into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We object to all intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To all intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since didn't -- at least don't see the people who produced them or who worked with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Ms. Stewart reminded me of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. McCloskey, there was an objection as to authenticity or at least lack of information of where it comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have his -- the comments, I think the substance of it relates to the events and the -- this critical issue of -- of where Colonel Blagojevic was. Clearly Colonel or General Keserovic could not have met with Colonel Blagojevic on the 18th if Colonel Blagojevic was at the Zepa theatre, so that's what the relevance of it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection was not about relevance. The objection was about background source and authenticity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, that's how you prove a document is authentic and real and the information in it is connected to the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But I understand the problem, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, if I would make a forgery I would always take care that it relates to what -- to the subject matter on which I want to make a forgery. So therefore, that seems not to be conclusive. We'll further think about it. If you have -- if you would do the same, and then we'll further deal with the matter at that moment and have it marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We do have the supervising person coming to testify about these things so we can wrap up some issues there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That may well resolve any questions about authenticity. So therefore, we mark it for identification. Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 21063C receives number P1581, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Do I understand under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it 21063 or is it 4081?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I get so much confirmation that it was the right number, that we leave it for the time being to that. If that would turn out to be wrong, we will correct it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This was my fault. I -- Judge Moloto's number was the document that we are dealing with a bit ahead of ourselves. So this is -- the number you mentioned, Your Honour, is a document, not an intercept. I had forgotten to offer the intercept into evidence. So 04081 is a new document that I want to ask the General about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is that document to be dealt with as a public document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. This is not an intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, just to fill out this 17 July period and the various orders, we can see that this is from the Special Police Brigade of the Ministry of Interior, and it's an order. Could we see whose name it's in? I think it's Saric. If we could just go to the bottom of the original? Yes. You've told us who that is. And we see here this order to search the terrain in the area of Pobudje sector on 17 July, mopping up, I won't read it all. It says Dusko Jevric is the commander. Have you ever heard of a Dusko Jevric or a Dusko Jevic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was a question for you, Mr. Keserovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't realise there was a question. I thought it was still part of the comment by Mr. McCloskey. I think it is Dusko Jevic, without the R, who at the time was an operative in the special MUP brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then we go to paragraph 4, it says that Borovcanin who will be in charge of command and control for both the combat groups that are described, and that -- is that the same Borovcanin you've talked about earlier?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that it says deputy commander, then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And does this order appear to be the -- the task that you spoke of when you saw Borovcanin yourself in the Bratunac area, that you've testified about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I saw Borovcanin and that the MUP forces were engaged in sweeping the terrain. That's all I know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Looking at the geography described in this document, does this appear to be the geography of the sweep operation that you were to be involved in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This task, when it says the right-hand side of the road to Milici, it is the area that was assigned to me in the original task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. General, let me just get right to the point that the indictment in this case is charged that the sweep operation on the 17th captured over 100 people and that they were summarily executed and buried in the Cerska valley. Had you been in command of those forces that did that sweep operation, would you bear any responsibility for the deaths of people captured in that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, it would be the responsibility of the operations commander, and the person who carried out the executions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And going to another topic, the topic that there was a discussion about your knowledge of international law, the Geneva Conventions, I don't want to spend a lot of time on that but I do want to see if you've seen one document, it's P1096. It's dated 1992, from the Main Staff of the armed forces of Republika Srpska. And it's from the military prosecutor's office at the Main Staff of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document was, I do understand, previously under seal but is now marked that it was not admitted. Just for your information. That's where we are with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Don't see any reason for it to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I don't have any recollection as to why it was not admitted but we'll find out later.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record I just put it's not now any more P1096. It's just 65 ter 4383.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's look at this same document but now under the number 65 ter 4383.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we are waiting for that, you have spoken briefly about the military police's job to prosecute crimes. You work with the military prosecutors in doing that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As unit commander, I was in contact with the military prosecutor's office and I cooperated with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. You can see what this is. Military staff of the armed forces of Republika Srpska, military prosecutor's office, the Main Staff of the armed forces, guidelines for determining the criteria for criminal prosecutions. And if we go through this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to page 3 in the English, which should be paragraph -- it's underlined paragraph 1, maybe -- it may be page 1 or 2 or 3 in the Serbian. Sorry, I don't have that. It's not that one obviously. It will be the underlined paragraph. Thank you. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we just see that one of the -- the first crime is the failure to respond to mobilisation and call-up. I think we can all agree that that's something important to have in time of war. But let's go on. Let's go to the next crime is the criminal offence of wilfully absenting one's self from one's post. I think that's pretty clear what that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But now let's go to it should be page 7 in the English and it's at paragraph 3, underlined paragraph in the Serbian, page 23 in the e-court English -- B/C/S, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are only nine pages in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I'm wrong about the English. But there we've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, as a career officer, an officer that clearly went through the ranks and is now a retired general, this important document in 1992, was this something that you saw?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was again a question for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We are almost done, general. That was a question.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple of things about it. "The legal classifications of the criminal offences from this chapter has been adopted from international conventions with some adaptation and closer definition. "In addition, legal descriptions of most of these offences refer to the application of rules of international law containing detailed regulations on illegality of certain acts so that only with the help of these rules can the full description of a relevant criminal offence be achieved. "The unique nature of these criminal offences is also in their seriousness which is expressed in severe punishments including the death penalty for six criminal offences. For some of these offences, such as genocide and war crimes, there is no time limit for criminal prosecution and punishment. "Crimes against humanity and international law can be committed by individuals acting on their own but by their nature these criminal offences are usually committed in an organised fashion in the implementation of the policy of the ruling circles. "Most of these criminal offences are committed only during armed conflicts or in some way closely connected with armed conflicts, which means that they are committed within the context of broad military operations and on orders from superior officers." Now, this basic clear explanation of international rules and laws was -- do you find any disagreements in that last paragraph? Is that something brand new to you? You said you didn't read about these things until 2011.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
