utterances.text: It doesn't refer to the instruction. I simply did not read the original Geneva Conventions in any previous period, acquainting myself with them in detail. There is nothing particularly new in this text, nothing that I hadn't known about in one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So has this information been around since 1949 and the Geneva Conventions and part of your training?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is only a matter of how reliably I can interpret the contents. However, I have a general understanding of the conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next page in English. "From this follows the explicit responsibility of the officer corps of the Army of Republika Srpska as the giver of orders in command of armed forces whose members could commit or are committing some of these offences, to take uncompromising action and prevent such conduct. This responsibility belongs by its nature, particularly to high-ranking individuals and officials in state, military or public organisations who are in the concrete circumstances in a position to issue orders." Is that your understanding of your training?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my first year of military academy, I had the course in the basics of international humanitarian and laws of war. It was in 1977 and 1978. Later on --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, excuse me, was this -- you can always explain your answer but simple question: Was the paragraph I just read, was that part of your training, as far as you remember? Recalling what you told us about 2011.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could say so. Part of the training, part of the education was such, and it applied to any and every officer who completed the military academy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, looking at the clock already for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask him about the next paragraph, if that was part of his training, and then if I could look at -- over the break and see if I have anything else left because I feel like I'm probably near the time that you want to hear from Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One thing before my learned friend continues, I don't understand -- I don't remember that I explored this area, so I don't know how redirect is emanating from my cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the knowledge of Geneva Conventions was dealt with by questions by the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I do remember that it was not general knowledge but it was mainly focused on prisoners of war rather than on general knowledge of the Geneva Conventions. If you just would deal with the next paragraph, do it briefly, and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The next paragraph, General: "If officers merely find out that units of the armed forces of the Army of Republika Srpska or their members have committed or are committing such acts, and take no measures to prevent the consequences or the acts themselves and expose perpetrators to criminal prosecution, this in itself makes them answerable for these criminal offences."

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the field of criminal liability, it would be a general rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is this in your view, one last question, an important rule in the military, this last one?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the instruction from the prosecutor's office or the rules in general in terms of one's duty to initiate proceedings as soon as it has been learned that there was a crime?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. The last paragraph I read, when you find out and don't do anything about it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, it is very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could try to organise myself at the break, I'm almost done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We do not object against organising yourself during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we take the break, I have one very short question. You said a couple of times that in 2011 you started studying in more detail the Geneva Conventions. What triggered you to do that in 2011? Was it in preparation for any testimony to be given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were several reasons. The first reason was that I was asked by the Defence team for Mr. Karadzic to comment on a number of provisions pertaining to the Manjaca camp which was part of Karadzic's indictment. Then, the prosecutor's office of Bosnia-Herzegovina asked me to provide comments about the functioning of the POW camp of the 5th Corps of the ABiH in Bihac. In addition to general military and security knowledge, I had to pinpoint the specific paragraphs which dealt with the topic. That was the reason. So nothing out of the ordinary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a break. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, we will briefly deal with two matters. The first was P1096 having been MFI'd first. There was an issue about authenticity at that time with that witness, and finally, on the -- I think it was -- on the 8th April, I read from the transcript. I said: "Finally, with regard to P1096, MFI, the Prosecution submits that this document will be tendered as a public exhibit through a different witness." And therefore, P1096 was vacated at the time. Now, we dealt with it with a different witness. I don't know whether this was the witness the Prosecution had in mind, but the authenticity concerns have not been resolved through this witness so that matter still stands. In view of what the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just want to say that that witness was a protected witness through whom this document was introduced, just to make everybody cautious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll not give any further details but, Mr. McCloskey, the authenticity concerns are expressed again by Mr. -- not now but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think Mr. McCloskey was not with us at that time at all, so I don't know how much he knows about the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you sort out whether this was the witness which the Prosecution had in mind to introduce the document with. There was another matter about intercepts where I have a redaction being made. Could the parties consider whether reading part of the intercept should remain confidential, because I think the reasons for these intercepts to be confidential do not in any way appear from the reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, that's correct. It's some of the information that's sometimes on the top or the bottom but the reading of it is normally not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then under those circumstances, I suggest to the parties that the redaction which was made earlier will be undone and that it will become part of the public record again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To the extent the document was shown as well, and that was also one of the reasons, because it's difficult to redact only what we see on the screens and the reading them becomes a part of that. So for these reasons, there would have been no reason to redact the transcript, but there is a reason to redact the video. And how we'll technically resolve this, Madam Registrar, will assist us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's whispered into my ear that the right solution would be that I hereby order that the transcript becomes public again but that the confidentiality of the video remains. That's hereby on the record. Apologies for continuing with matters, Mr. Keserovic, that are not related to your testimony. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Very briefly, General, if you receive an order over the telephone from General Mladic from Belgrade, would you follow it? A perfectly legitimate, reasonable order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could identify the person as being General Mladic beyond any doubt, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if General Mladic entered an agreement with an international organisation while he was in Belgrade that committed the, let's say in your situation, the security organ to some procedure, would that be valid? And would the security organ follow through with what he agreed to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid that I'm not competent enough for that area because it is in the realm of the relations with foreigners. Nobody can draw somebody else into some sort of a relationship with foreigners, international organisations, unless that is part and parcel of the state policy or, in other words, it is not up to the army to introduce this or translated into orders or actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, this is what happens if you put a question of such a hypothetical nature, then you get these kind of answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It wasn't a great question, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'm looking forward to your next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, has the re-examination triggered any need for further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was pretty lengthy so it does trigger some.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, no, no. I can't say it does come as a surprise that you have further questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, I did promise that I will have no more questions for you, but unfortunately there are certain issue that we need to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to tender statement of this witness that has 65 ter number 25999, and if it would please the Court, we can do the selection so we don't -- do not dump the whole document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How long is this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The statement is approximately 80 pages, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we certainly prefer that you make a selection.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So I -- we will just extract the pages we used during the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then upload it later and give an opportunity to the Prosecution to add anything to contextualise the portions you have selected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President, because once that is done then there are the Blagojevic transcripts, which contextualise it, there is the Tolimir transcripts, and then we end up battling transcripts. That's why it's not normally appropriate for something this important, but -- I can certainly do that and we can try to reach a smaller pages in the battling of transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But my learned friend remembers that he introduced some pages from Tolimir transcript already through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We will get together on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. We will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would say a cup of coffee or a cup of tea, still to be determined. Yes, we will wait. You put to the witness what you want to put to him at this moment and then later we'll hear the results of your conversations what --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to proceed with this statement any more, at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we are waiting for your further initiatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First I would like to see D129.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we are about to see a document which was shown to you by the prosecutor. It's a document issued by the Ministry of the Interior. You were asked to give your comments on it. The date is 10th of July, 1995. Have a look at the document, please. Is it correct that the document indicates that the MUP forces are not resubordinated to the VRS forces in the operations envisaged in this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is Tomislav Kovac who issued these forces with their assignments. He was either deputy minister of the interior or minister of the interior at the time. So it is in that capacity that he issued orders to these units. When I said that they were resubordinated, I had in mind item 5 which said that the commander of the unit is duty-bound upon arriving in the area to get in touch with the commander of the corps or with the commander of the four -- of the corps, and I suppose that I thought this -- of this as resubordination, but this is actually placement under the command of the commander of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We no longer need the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have P1580? This document was discussed today as 65 ter 4477.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You can see that it's a report of the ICRC. Mention was made of the evacuation of the wounded on the 17th and the 18th. In answer to these questions, you said that all these wounded individuals were within the jurisdiction of the army. In the town of Bratunac, who was in charge of enforcing law and order and arraigning perpetrators of crimes? Was it within the purview of military or civilian bodies?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the police that is charged with enforcement of law and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Civilian police, you mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If, in addition -- or, rather, if civilian policemen were by these wounded individuals, would it be the civilian police or the army that would be responsible for these wounded individuals?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if the police was providing security for them, they would be responsible for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And even if the town is within the area of responsibility of someone, it is the civilian police that has the competence for providing security within that area, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we briefly look at P1581C, or 65 ter 121063C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I seek some further explanation of the previous question and answer. I think I put a few questions to you in relation to those wounded, and I asked you whether you would agree with me that those who were not free to go, whether you would consider them prisoners of war. And I think you agreed to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting you. This one is under seal, this document, so it shouldn't be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, the -- not to be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was just warned by my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine. I go back to -- yes, but I can imagine you urgently wanted to draw our attention to the confidential character of that document. You agreed with me that you considered them to be prisoners of war. Now, in the last answer, it was suggested to you that the police being charged with enforcement of law and order, civilian police, that they would be in charge of enforcing law and order and arraigning perpetrators of crimes. Would you say that the civilian police is responsible for the treatment of prisoners of war, or is it that even if someone is a prisoner of war, that he is not exempted from possible investigation by the civilian police on any crime he is suspected of? Which of the two, or any third option, did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say that they were within the jurisdiction of the civilian police at the time. Rather, the question was if the civilian police was securing them, would that mean that they would be within their jurisdiction, and my answer was yes, they would be. Now, if you'll allow me, I won't take long. There were cases, a specific one in 1992, in the municipality of Prijedor, where three collection centres or camps - Keraterm, Trnopolje, and Omarska - were placed in the hands of the civilian police, whereas the Manjaca camp was under the army. This depended on the prevailing circumstances and conditions and who it was who was given the assignment, so in view of these considerations, I could not rule out the possibility that the police could provide security for and be responsible for prisoners of war. I stand by that, that the commander of the military unit within whose area the prisoners of war are present is responsible for them, but I also do not rule out the possibility that someone could have decided otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to understand your answer, do you say that the military commander who was responsible for the prisoners of war can just say, "Now you police, from now on, you're responsible. I'm not responsible anymore but you are"? I see you're nodding no. Do I understand, then, that the police playing a role --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The commander could not transfer the responsibility. This could have been decided upon by superiors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which superior could do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the level of the Supreme Command, it could have been the case and it should have been the case, and this is most often the case, that the decision is taken as to who would be responsible. Would it be the VRS or the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that all in relation to prisoners of war? Can the Supreme Command -- I can imagine that you say you, MUP, assist us in avoiding that our prisoners of war will escape, to come to our assistance, but is it your position that the military command, highest commands, can just move the responsibility for the prisoners of war to police forces which are not part of the military command structure? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The military forces themselves cannot shift responsibility. It may so happen that responsibility is transferred on to the police but it cannot be done by the commander within the zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it can be done by the Supreme Commander, if the Supreme Commander of the forces which is, if I understand the situation well, is the president of the republic? He can say, "Well, you army people, you took prisoners of war, and now the police is responsible for them from now on"? And they would still be prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They would still be prisoners of war. It's just that the police or the Ministry of the Interior would be responsible for them because, after all, they are part and parcel of the armed forces in times of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the police as a structure of the armed forces, not in any other capacity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The police just being part of the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The army is one unit and the police is the other. But together they formed the armed forces of a republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand what your position is. I have no further questions, I think in relation to that, apart from one matter. Yes. In one of your previous answers you said the following, and I don't know whether I fully understood it, therefore I'll read it to you again. You were talking about the document that was shown to you, especially paragraph 5 in which it says: "Upon arrival, get in touch with the --" you remember the document that was about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, with Colonel Krstic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- yes, it's about -- yes. Now, you said the following: "I suppose that I thought this -- of this as resubordination, but this is actually placement under the command of the commander of the Drina Corps." That is how it was translated to us. Could you clarify what you exactly meant there? Is it resubordination or is it not resubordination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From this term, "get in touch," I understood this actually to mean the resubordination to the commander of the Drina Corps because resubordination in essence means placement under the command. That was my opinion based on what I was able to read here. I'm not sure that this was reflected in the situation on the ground, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I now see, therefore, that for you, actually placing yourself under the command of is resubordination and that's what you read to be meant in paragraph 5 of that document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be brief, General. I want to go back to something. Since police forces can also be tasked with issuing IDs or arresting the perpetrators of crimes, or scene of crime techniques, is it correct that police forces can be under the command and control of the army only if resubordinated to a military command for the purposes of a particular operation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Only if resubordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that resubordination is a strictly prescribed activity which needs to include information on one unit being resubordinated to another unit and the word "resubordination" or "shall be resubordinated" must be present?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the key term.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I placed this topic on the screen. It deals with another topic. It has to do with the column of buses setting off. You tried to explain something when you said that Zepa was still within the area. What area? The area of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the time it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How far is Zepa from Bratunac, approximately, or from the outer part of the area of the Bratunac Brigade or its command post?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Srebrenica to Zepa, I think there is less than ten kilometres because the enclaves were very close by. They basically bordered on each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This question may sound simplistic but I still have to put it: Is it possible for someone to go to Zepa on the 17th and be in Bratunac back on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. That is also an issue that has been bothering me all along.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we next see document number 04081?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Once we have it on the screen, we'll discuss resubordination yet again. That is to say the resubordination of police units to the army. This document dates -- is dated the 17th of July, 1995. It was issued by the Special Police Brigade. Have a look at it and tell us whether under this document the police in the field in that area is resubordinated to the army or is not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can see from the document that the special brigade commander ordered or issued tasks to his unit, so we cannot see that they were resubordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This search operation, had it begun before this date? I think you've already mentioned that in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it had.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I'm about to conclude. My learned friend, Mr. McCloskey, asked you this: When Mladic issues an order by phone, would it be carried out? We could see on the footage that General Mladic was on the phone at the military medical academy. I think we interrupted at that point. But General Mladic was on the phone at the military medical academy, the call went to Republika Srpska, and he ordered some vehicles. The fact that he was using an open line, does it point to the fact that he did not have any communications equipment with him; in other words, was he duty-bound to use communications equipment under the rules before resorting to an open line? Do you know what the regulation is in terms of such situations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That assumes a fact not in evidence. There has been no evidence that this is an open line. We don't have an intercept of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all I only intervened at your second question about a hypothetical question. I think the first one was as hypothetical - if Mr. Mladic would give an order by phone - not related to any factual situation. I was already about at that moment, but then the witness gave a short answer. Apparently he had an idea about what it was. It was only the second question that I intervened. That second question was hypothetical just as the first one was. Now, Mr. Lukic, what you're doing now, you're introducing all kind of facts and perhaps assumptions or is it still hypothetical? If it's hypothetical, then you should say, if he gives an order by public phone, would you follow that? If he gives an order by anything else, that -- it's still hypothetical, so I would rather hear from the witness whether it ever happened and whether he -- did you ever receive any order by telephone, either public or non-public through the form of communications channels? Did you ever receive an order by telephone from Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Neither from him, nor from the corps commanders who were my superiors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I allowed -- I didn't intervene in one hypothetical question, so, Mr. Lukic, if you insist to put a hypothetical question to the witness then the equality of arms is restored.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll just put an another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- actually it's the second part of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are there any rules in terms of sequence on how communications should be used?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are rules on communications, including the sequence of their use. Only in extraordinary urgent situations, when no delay is allowed, when every minute counts, when it is already obvious what is going on, then an order can be conveyed openly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. This would be all on our part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I had forgot to offer this document that's in -- on the screen into evidence. It should be 65 ter 4081, and so I would do that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that was, what is on our screen at this moment? If --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of course, no objections. We used it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. Madam Registrar the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 4081 receives number P1582, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1582 is admitted into evidence. Further, Mr. McCloskey, going back to P1581, that is an intercept which was not shown to the public, you used that document in your efforts to establish what happened on the 17th. Now, if you look at the original, you'll find that there is a date on it, English translation has no date. So if you want the Chamber to rely on the date, which seems to be the core matter, then I would suggest that you upload a full translation, including the heading which bears a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We'll do that. We have been in a bit of a tussle over that procedurally because in order to identify the date on these print-outs, you have to have many pages before you get to the date because they are sent out in reports, but we will be able to do that and make some sense of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, the original covers two pages, with the relevant heading with the date. The English translation covers two pages, same content, but not the heading. So ... I'm not yet convinced by this rather complex --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a bigger picture, Your Honour, which if we have to wait until we all have a good night's sleep to deal with, but it's a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. McCloskey, just the B/C/S uploaded has a date. The English translation has not a translation of that date, to the extent you have to translate dates, but the header is not there with a date. If you think you can do without, then the Chamber might rely on this document and finally conclude that it does not in any way support what you intended to establish because there is no date on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand, and we'll of course fix that simple problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's just related to another problem which I'll talk about on another day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would say fix the simple problem and then all the other problems we'll hear about later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One last one because there is one more document that I need to offer that I had forgotten to offer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 65 ter 13880. That was the 18 July Kijac document. That mentioned the evacuation on two days, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No objections? Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 13880 receives number P1583, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1583 is admitted into evidence. Nothing further? Then, Mr. Keserovic, there concludes your testimony in this Court. I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you either by the parties or by the Bench.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness? I do understand that no protective measures. Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We are, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the next witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I be excused for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, witness. Can you hear me in a language you understand? Apparently yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the rules require that you make a solemn declaration, the text is now handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, please be seated. Witness, you'll first be examined by Mr. Vanderpuye. Mr. Vanderpuye, you find him to your right, and he is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Vanderpuye you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much Mr. President, good afternoon to you and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Salapura.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I did neglect to ask the Chamber for a Rule 90(E) caution. One was issued previously with respect to the Colonel's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Salapura, I'd like to inform you of Rule 90(E) of this Tribunal which states that a witness, that means in this situation you, that you may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate yourself, if you do so. The Chamber, however, may compel you to answer the question, but if we would do that, testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against you, apart from if that would be a prosecution for giving false testimony. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. Vanderpuye, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you again, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, let me start with this: Could you state your name for the record, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Petar Salapura.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness kindly be asked to lean back and refrain from touching the console as it creates background noise? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please lean a bit back? Perhaps -- and could you refrain from touching something which creates noise for our interpreters? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Colonel, do you recall testifying in the case of the Prosecutor versus Tolimir on the 2nd through the 5th and the 9th of May 2011?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was the testimony that you gave at that time truthful and accurate to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. It is possible that some dates may be questionable but it's been a long time ago and perhaps I can't remember everything, but the rest is fully accurate and truthful.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well we'll deal with some of that in just a little bit. Did you have an opportunity to listen to your testimony, an audio recording of it, prior to testifying here today?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And having listened to your testimony, does it faithfully reflect what you said during the -- during your testimony in the Tolimir case?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I'll talk to you -- I'll ask you a little bit in just a minute about the date question that you've just raised, but in substance, is your testimony as you gave it in the Tolimir case how you would answer questions concerning the same issues if they were put to you in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How do you wish to clarify it at this time in terms of when you first became aware of the involvement of the members of the 10th sabotage detachment in these crimes?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have a summary I'd like to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think so, yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll take a break after you've read the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. In July 1995, Colonel Petar Salapura was the chief of the VRS Main Staff's intelligence administration. His immediate superior was General Tolimir, the assistant commander for security and intelligence and chief of the sector which also comprised the security administration led by Colonel Ljubisa Beara. Colonel Salapura's evidence concerns, among other things, the structure of the security and intelligence sector, its constituent administrations, their relationships to subordinate professional organs, and their reporting obligations and practices. Colonel Salapura exercised specialist or professional control over intelligence organs in subordinate formations toward the 410th Intelligence Centre and toward the 10th Sabotage Detachment, which he describes as an independent Main Staff unit directly subordinated to General Mladic. In June 1995, Colonel Salapura vetted a plan to engage the 10th Sabotage Detachment in an attack in Srebrenica town. Initially requested by members of the Drina Corps command, including Colonel Beara's professional subordinate Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic and Colonel Salapura's professional subordinate, Major Pavle Golic. Colonel Salapura proposed the mission to General Mladic upon whose approval and order it was carried out. There were civilian casualties. When Srebrenica fell, Colonel Salapura was in Banja Luka. On the morning of 13 July 1995, he set off for the Main Staff command in Han Pijesak from Bijeljina to inform General Mladic urgently of certain intelligence information. He stopped at the 65th Protection Regiment's MP Battalion command at Nova Kasaba where he observed prisoners at the football stadium. MP Battalion Commander Major Malin -- Zoran Malinic, informed Colonel Salapura that General Mladic was in the Bratunac area. Colonel Salapura eventually caught up with General Mladic. He was filmed with him in Srebrenica. Colonel Salapura later headed to Han Pijesak passing through Potocari where he saw women and children being loaded onto buses. He reached the VRS command in the afternoon where he remained actively engaged in his work through 18 July 1995. Colonel Salapura admitted later learning of the involvement of members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment in the Srebrenica-related executions from the unit's commander, Milorad Pelemis. He claimed he was "horrified by it" and "couldn't really get a grasp on the number of people, something like that -- something like that was possible, the scale." Still, he claimed their involvement was involuntary. In January 1996, he requested the RS Minister of the Interior, Dragan Kijac, to issue false identifications for members of the unit implicated in these crimes. Mr. President, that concludes my summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. We take a break first. Witness, we will take a break of 20 minutes and we'll have some other 20 minutes left after the break. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Thank you. A small error or typo slipped in. The operation you mention in the month of June was a sabotage action. It was carried out on the 22nd. At any rate in late June. There were no victims, or there was one woman, but it was not established how her death came about. There was the first report by UNPROFOR and then the information services of the 28th Division indicated that there were no casualties. The action was a diversionary one because of the prevailing weather conditions. There was fog.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right, Colonel. Thank you for that clarification, and I think the Chamber has at its disposal the evidence relating to the subject matter of the operation itself and the question of casualties and so forth. As I mentioned to you yesterday, I wanted to try to be as brief as possible with you in your direct examination. So I just wanted to show you a few documents and hopefully proceed in that way. First, can I just confirm with you that the rules that were applied during the period of time that you were in the VRS Main Staff were rules that were established in the JNA and adopted?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'd like to show you is 65 ter 4643 and it relates to the intelligence support of the armed forces. It's a 1987 manual. I hope we will have the translation up in a moment. Are you familiar with this particular manual or this particular document, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in principle, was this document used in discharging your duties as the chief of the intelligence administration in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. But I also had to adapt to the prevailing circumstances. The document was drafted in peacetime and for what was perhaps a different sort of warfare. It was drafted as part of preparations for the defence of Yugoslavia in the event of an aggression -- of an external aggression, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: My question is, then, did it form the basis of the rules that you applied as the chief of the intelligence administration in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. We proceeded from them. We -- that was our starting point.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have spoken with the Defence to determine whether or not there was any objection to the admission of this document. I understand that there isn't so I would tender it at this time. I can go through more elements of it, but I think it would be quicker to do it this way.

utterances.text: That's very quick but it's also 117 pages, Mr. Vanderpuye, of which we do not know yet where and what will become relevant for us.

utterances.text: I can identify those at a later point if you would like me to MFI it now, or I can lead the witness through those points.

utterances.text: No. If -- there is no need to do that, but to say here you have got 117 pages, we need a bit of -- you say you'll sooner or later draw our attention to specific portions which -- let me --

utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, if there is no objection from the Defence, then there is no need yet at this moment to tender it. You don't intend to ask any further questions to the witness. And then make the appropriate selections. Not having looked at the document, I know already there are many paragraphs which are totally irrelevant for us I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And if you therefore -- even MFI'ing now, there is no objection against it being admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Make a selection, speak to the Defence about what the Defence considers relevant, and then bring the selection to our attention and tender it, and we'll then most likely admit that selection.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. What I'll do then is I'll move to the next document, which is 65 ter 25993.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is a shorter document but the same principal would apply, so let me ask you, Colonel, and this document may seem familiar to you, and it's called instructions for land-based diversionary operations, and let me ask again was this document adapted by the VRS Main Staff and formed the basis for the rules that were applicable during your tenure as chief of the intelligence administration with respect to sabotage units and, in particular, the 10th Sabotage Detachment of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: This document was only the basis. We didn't have our own instructions and we didn't have time to draft them. We used this manual as a basis only.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is a shorter document, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's 18 pages. I would -- you're suggested to take the same procedure which is fully supported by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Give us whatever we need. Don't give us what we don't need.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. All right. Then I'll move on. It's clear for the record what it is, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And no objections I take it then as well. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Colonel, I just wanted to ask you very briefly some questions about the history of the security and intelligence sector. In 1992, was there a security and intelligence sector in the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. As the Main Staff was set up, I think the intelligence and security administration was established first. This because we had very few men and were unable to create separate services. At a later stage, with some additional recruitment, we had two separate administrations, security administration and intelligence administration. This was later transformed into a sector headed by General Tolimir which consisted of two administrations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I just want to make sure that the record is clear because my question was whether or not there was a sector in 1992. You said that there was; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. I think so. I think that the sector was already established back in 1992. May, June. I think so, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And initially in 1992, to whom was the chief of intelligence subordinated?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: In the beginning of 1992, this was within the military district, and it was still called the department for intelligence affairs. I was the chief of that department, and I was subordinated to the Chief of Staff of the military district. As for the security department, it was subordinated to the commander of the military district. As the military district was transformed, that's to say as the command of the military district was transformed into the Main Staff of the VRS, these departments became administrations. So we came to have the security administration and the intelligence administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When the military district became the -- was transformed into the Main Staff of the VRS, as you say, to whom were you immediately subordinated at that time, that is, at the initial -- at the initiation of the VRS Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Initially to the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When the administrations were formed under the sector of security and intelligence, to whom were you, as the chief of the intelligence administration, immediately subordinate?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: To General Tolimir, the chief of sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And just so we are clear, in terms of the security administration of the Main Staff, to whom was the chief of that administration subordinated at the time that the two administrations were created under the sector?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: To the chief of sector who was at the same time assistant commander for intelligence and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Again, is that General Tolimir or was that General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: General Tolimir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just want to clarify one other thing and that is you indicated in your testimony at page 13486 that the 10th Sabotage Detachment was an independent unit of the Main Staff. First, can you tell us what that means?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: It was an autonomous unit of the Main Staff. Now, I don't know how it comes across when it's translated into English. Rather than independent, it's an autonomous unit and as such it was subordinate to the chief of the Main Staff. It was not under the Protection Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to clarify a couple of things. First, my question, and I refer to your testimony at page 13486, so the record should just reflect that that concerns the testimony in the Tolimir case. And the second thing I want to clarify is what you've said here, that it was an autonomous unit subordinate to the chief of the Main Staff. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: For the detachment? No, I said the commander of the Main Staff. And under the professional line, to the chief of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: So that's the use of manpower, personnel, recruitment, supplies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreters did not get the whole of your answer. Could you resume where you said for the detachment -- no --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I said recruitment, training and education of manpower, and supplying units with the necessary assets to carry out the specific assignments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would wait next time exactly to what I'm asking you. The interpreters got lost a bit earlier. You said: "For the detachment? No, I said the commander of the Main Staff. And under the professional line, to the chief of --" And what did you then say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In terms of professional control, to the chief of the intelligence administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was what was missing. Please proceed, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just want to clarify a couple of things before we break. Where the detachment is used for actions that are not strictly part of their normal assignment, is that something that only the commander of the Main Staff could order?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA
utterances.text: Yes. The chief of administration cannot order that. It -- he can only propose, but only under the professional line, so they can be assignments related to diversionary actions, sabotage, or reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see we've got about a minute left and I'm about to go to a different part, as brief as I had hoped it would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wouldn't do it, Mr. Vanderpuye. I would just enjoy the break, coming --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would very much like to do that.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is clear.

utterances.text: Then we'll deal with that and we'll not bother the witness with that. Mr. Salapura, we would like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, it is a short administrative matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I should inform the Chamber that we now have a copy of the CD related to P1587 that was MFI'd and was the video clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And there is no objection. Therefore, the status of P1587 changes into an -- admitted into evidence as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
